turn_text: We have on the line with us out from Washington this morning is U.S. Senator Tina Smith. Senator, thank you so much for joining us today.
Good morning, Jeff. I'm so glad to be with you.

Yeah, we're going to talk today about EMS services in rural sections of Minnesota because you've been working on some things and talking with some people. First of all, can you, I guess, give us an idea of some of the things that you've heard while you've been holding some sessions with workers in rural Minnesota. Where are we at? Kind of a crisis situation.

I really think we have a big challenge on our hands. I start from the place that no matter where you live in Minnesota, when you dial 911, because you have an emergency, you need help. You need to trust that someone is going to be able to get to you as soon as they can to help you with whatever your emergency is. In rural parts of our state and small towns and rural areas, Oftentimes, folks are relying on volunteer rural EMS services to do that work and to get them to the hospital or to help them when they need help. But those rural systems are under a lot of pressure. We've been doing discussions all over the state and have heard how challenged they are by lack of volunteer, very poor reimbursement for their costs for getting patients the care that they need, and it's really reached a crisis in the state and many parts of the state.
Are you hearing from your fellow senators that that is an issue? I would imagine if this happening in Minnesota is probably happening in a lot of areas of rural U.S. Have you heard much about that?

Yes, you're absolutely right. This is not just a Minnesota problem. It's happening all over the place and many senators who represent large rural communities are experiencing the same thing. And I want to point out that the Minnesota State Legislature and Governor Wals have established a statewide rural EMS task force to look at state solutions to this because the answers are going to be part of federal government and part of what the state and local communities can do. And, you know, I'm hearing from these rural EMS providers that They are, you know, people are working extremely long hours. And here's an interesting thing and a big problem they have. If you go, many of them rely on getting reimbursement from Medicare for their trips because most of the people who live in rural communities and who need ambulance are often covered by Medicare. But if you make a trip to somebody's house and you're able to help them without taking them to a hospital, then you don't get any reimbursement at all. And that's putting a huge strain on them. So I'm working on legislation with my colleague from Vermont to help to at least fix that problem.
Let's get into some more specifics about the bill. What is it going to look like? And is it still, I guess, under construction? Are you still writing it?

Well, so we have written the bill and introduced it. We introduced it several weeks ago. And our hope will be to move it through the Senate process so that we can get it signed into law. And it would be an adjustment to the Medicare, how Medicare pays for services. I think, I mean, it's got good bipartisan support. People can really appreciate this. And they can appreciate that just because you don't end up taking somebody to a hospital shouldn't mean that you're not reimbursed for the really important care that you provide. As an example of what this means, I hear from rural EMS providers that they are reimbursed for barely half of the cost of their trips. You've got an ambulance or a vehicle, you've got gas, and even if the people who are driving that vehicle are working almost for free because their volunteers, their costs are still not getting covered.
